options.a: Use a recovery cylinder rated for 400 psig instead of a standard tank
options.b: Add a moisture-indicating sight glass at the recovery machine outlet
options.c: Install an in-line filter drier ahead of the recovery machine inlet
options.d: Change the recovery machine's compressor oil after the job is finished

distractorExplanations.a: A higher cylinder pressure rating does nothing to stop acid and moisture from reaching the recovery machine's compressor.
distractorExplanations.b: A sight glass only indicates moisture, and at the outlet it is downstream of the machine it is supposed to protect.
distractorExplanations.d: An oil change after the job is a cleanup step; it does not keep acid and moisture out of the machine during recovery.

options.a: Chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) and hydrochlorofluorocarbons (HCFCs)
options.b: Hydrofluoroolefins (HFOs) and hydrocarbon refrigerants like R-290
options.c: Ammonia (R-717) and carbon dioxide (R-744) natural refrigerants
options.d: Volatile organic compounds (VOCs) and ground-level ozone precursors

distractorExplanations.b: HFOs and hydrocarbons have zero ODP and very low GWP; they are substitutes, not the ozone-depleting classes regulated here.
distractorExplanations.c: Ammonia and CO2 have zero ozone depletion potential and are exempt from the venting prohibition, so they are not the target class.
distractorExplanations.d: VOCs are smog precursors controlled under the CAA criteria-pollutant programs, not stratospheric ozone protection under Title VI.

options.a: Hearing protection and a disposable N95 dust mask
options.b: Safety glasses and chemical-resistant gloves
options.c: Hard hat and steel-toed boots for cylinder handling
options.d: A face shield alone with standard cotton work gloves

distractorExplanations.a: An N95 filters particulates, not refrigerant vapor, and hearing protection does nothing against frostbite or eye injury from liquid refrigerant.
distractorExplanations.c: Hard hats and boots address falling objects and dropped cylinders, not eye and skin exposure to escaping refrigerant.
distractorExplanations.d: Cotton gloves soak up liquid refrigerant and hold it against the skin, causing frostbite; safety glasses and resistant gloves are needed.

options.a: Using separate recovery cylinders for each refrigerant type
options.b: Using one recovery cylinder for refrigerants of the same safety class
options.c: Running the recovery machine's self-purge only at the end of the day
options.d: Combining refrigerants with similar pressures in one recovery cylinder

distractorExplanations.b: Sharing an A1 safety class does not make refrigerants compatible; mixing any two types in one cylinder contaminates both.
distractorExplanations.c: The machine must be purged between refrigerant types on each job; a single end-of-day purge carries residue into the next cylinder.
distractorExplanations.d: Similar pressure-temperature curves do not make refrigerants mixable; any blend of types becomes a contaminated mixture.

options.a: To phase down HFC production as its original 1987 treaty objective
options.b: To phase out production and consumption of ozone-depleting substances
options.c: To set binding greenhouse-gas emission targets for industrial nations
options.d: To require technician certification for anyone handling refrigerants

distractorExplanations.a: The HFC phasedown came with the 2016 Kigali Amendment; the 1987 treaty targeted ozone-depleting substances.
distractorExplanations.c: Binding greenhouse-gas targets for industrial nations describe the Kyoto Protocol, not the Montreal Protocol.
distractorExplanations.d: Technician certification is a U.S. Clean Air Act Section 608 requirement, not the purpose of the international treaty.

options.a: The number of fluorine atoms bonded to each carbon in the molecule
options.b: The presence of chlorine atoms in the molecular structure
options.c: The refrigerant's GWP rating relative to carbon dioxide
options.d: The refrigerant's boiling point and saturation pressure at 70°F

distractorExplanations.a: Fluorine does not destroy stratospheric ozone; HFCs are fully fluorinated yet have zero ODP because they lack chlorine.
distractorExplanations.c: GWP measures heat trapping relative to CO2; it is a separate metric and HFCs show high GWP with zero ODP.
distractorExplanations.d: Boiling point and pressure define the appliance class (low/high pressure), not how much ozone the molecule destroys.

options.a: When the recovery cylinder reaches 60% of its rated liquid capacity
options.b: When they suspect the presence of mixed refrigerants in the system
options.c: When the ambient temperature exceeds 90°F while recovery is running
options.d: When the recovery machine pulls the system into an inches-of-mercury vacuum

distractorExplanations.a: The fill limit is 80% of capacity by weight; 60% is still within the safe range and is no reason to stop work.
distractorExplanations.c: High ambient temperature calls for watching cylinder pressure, but it is not a stop-and-escalate trigger like suspected mixed refrigerant.
distractorExplanations.d: Pulling the system into a vacuum is the normal goal of recovery, not a sign that something is wrong.

options.a: The refrigerant distributor selling the cylinder
options.b: An EPA-approved certifying organization
options.c: The state contractor licensing board
options.d: The technician's employer after on-the-job training

distractorExplanations.a: Distributors must verify a buyer's certification card, but they do not test or certify technicians.
distractorExplanations.c: State licensing boards issue contractor licenses; Section 608 certification comes from EPA-approved certifying organizations.
distractorExplanations.d: Employers cannot issue Section 608 certification; the technician must pass a test from an EPA-approved certifying program.

options.a: Refrigerants with higher molecular weight have greater ozone depletion potential
options.b: The presence of hydrogen atoms generally reduces ozone depletion potential
options.c: Fluorine atoms in refrigerants directly contribute to stratospheric ozone destruction
options.d: Carbon-carbon double bonds increase both ozone depletion and global warming potential

distractorExplanations.a: ODP depends on chlorine (or bromine) content and atmospheric lifetime, not molecular weight; heavy HFCs still have zero ODP.
distractorExplanations.c: Fluorine atoms do not directly destroy ozone; chlorine and bromine atoms are the primary ozone-depleting species released from refrigerants.
distractorExplanations.d: Carbon-carbon double bonds actually tend to make molecules more reactive and shorter-lived, potentially reducing their environmental impact.

options.a: To ensure technicians can properly install and commission new HVAC equipment
options.b: To prevent the release of ozone-depleting substances during service and repair
options.c: To make HVAC systems meet DOE minimum energy efficiency standards
options.d: To license contractors who bid on commercial refrigeration and HVAC projects

distractorExplanations.a: Installation skill is covered by trade licensing; Section 608 certification targets refrigerant release during service.
distractorExplanations.c: Efficiency minimums are DOE appliance standards; Section 608 deals with refrigerant emissions, not efficiency.
distractorExplanations.d: Section 608 certifies individual technicians, not contractor businesses, and has nothing to do with bidding.

options.a: Purging the recovery cylinder with nitrogen before beginning recovery
options.b: Venting non-condensables from the system low side before connecting
options.c: Monitoring recovery cylinder pressure and temperature throughout the process
options.d: Adding refrigerant oil to the recovery machine before starting to protect its compressor

distractorExplanations.d: Pre-oiling the recovery machine does not address non-condensables; the hazard is rising cylinder pressure, which must be monitored.
distractorExplanations.b: Venting from the system releases refrigerant with the air and is prohibited; non-condensables are handled at the recovery cylinder.
distractorExplanations.a: Purging with nitrogen is not a standard practice and could introduce additional non-condensables into the system.

options.a: The mixed refrigerant can be reused in any compatible system after proper filtration
options.b: The refrigerant mixture must be destroyed or reclaimed to ARI-700 standards before reuse
options.c: Only the R-22 portion needs to be reclaimed; the R-134a can be vented safely
options.d: The mixture can be separated using standard recovery equipment and reused immediately

distractorExplanations.a: Mixed refrigerants have altered thermodynamic properties and cannot be safely reused even with filtration, as this doesn't address the fundamental contamination issue.
distractorExplanations.c: All regulated refrigerants, including R-134a, are subject to EPA venting prohibitions and cannot be released to the atmosphere regardless of contamination status.
distractorExplanations.d: Standard recovery equipment cannot effectively separate different refrigerant types, and even if separation were possible, the refrigerants would still require proper reclamation before reuse.

options.a: CFCs only, since HCFCs were exempted as transitional refrigerants
options.b: CFCs, HCFCs, and their substitutes including HFCs
options.c: HCFCs and HFOs, with CFCs covered under a separate production ban
options.d: Natural refrigerants such as ammonia, CO2 and hydrocarbons

distractorExplanations.a: HCFCs such as R-22 are ozone-depleting and fully covered by Section 608, not exempted as transitional refrigerants.
distractorExplanations.c: CFCs are covered by Section 608 servicing rules too, and HFOs are low-GWP substitutes rather than ozone-depleting substances.
distractorExplanations.d: Ammonia, CO2 and most hydrocarbons have zero ODP and are exempt from the venting prohibition in many uses.

options.a: Use the equipment as-is, since the small R-22 residue is within AHRI 700 purity limits
options.b: Flush the recovery equipment with nitrogen and vent it before switching refrigerant types
options.c: Evacuate the recovery equipment to remove residual refrigerant, then purge with the new refrigerant type
options.d: Change the filter-drier and hoses, then connect directly to the R-134a system without evacuating

distractorExplanations.a: AHRI 700 is a reclaim purity standard, not a tolerance for residue; leftover R-22 contaminates the R-134a.
distractorExplanations.b: A nitrogen flush does not pull residual refrigerant and oil out of the machine and venting it releases refrigerant.
distractorExplanations.d: New hoses and a filter-drier do not remove R-22 left in the machine's compressor and condenser; evacuation is still needed.

options.a: Continue recovery since the pressure is still below the maximum rating
options.b: Stop recovery immediately and allow the cylinder to cool before continuing
options.c: Open the cylinder vapor valve briefly to vent pressure down to 300 psig
options.d: Switch to a larger recovery cylinder, since more internal volume lowers pressure

distractorExplanations.c: Venting vapor from a recovery cylinder releases refrigerant and is prohibited; cooling the cylinder lowers pressure.
distractorExplanations.d: A cylinder holding liquid and vapor sits at saturation pressure set by temperature, not by cylinder volume.
distractorExplanations.a: This ignores the safety margin needed below maximum working pressure and risks equipment damage or safety hazards.

options.a: A2L flammability classification requiring new safety standards
options.b: High chemical toxicity that triggers OSHA exposure-limit rules
options.c: High global warming potential contributing to climate change
options.d: Long atmospheric lifetime that lets them reach and thin the ozone layer

distractorExplanations.a: R-134a and R-410A are A1 (nonflammable); the A2L class applies to newer low-GWP options like R-32 and R-454B.
distractorExplanations.b: Both are low-toxicity A1 refrigerants; EPA HFC rules under the AIM Act are driven by GWP, not toxicity.
distractorExplanations.d: HFCs contain no chlorine, so they do not deplete ozone regardless of lifetime; their concern is climate impact.

options.a: Continue with recovery using the expired equipment since it was previously certified
options.b: Use the equipment only if it passes a visual inspection for obvious defects
options.c: Obtain properly certified recovery equipment before beginning any recovery operations
options.d: Proceed if the system holds under 15 pounds, then recertify the equipment afterward

distractorExplanations.d: There is no small-charge exemption to the recovery equipment certification requirement; 15 pounds is unrelated here.
distractorExplanations.a: Previous certification does not authorize continued use once expired; current valid certification is mandatory for all recovery operations.
distractorExplanations.b: Visual inspection cannot substitute for proper certification; EPA requires formal certification that includes performance testing and verification.

options.a: De minimis leak - no repair required
options.b: Substantial leak requiring repair within 30 days
options.c: Critical leak requiring immediate shutdown
options.d: Minor leak requiring repair within 12 months

distractorExplanations.a: This leak rate far exceeds de minimis levels, which are typically under 10% annually for most systems.
distractorExplanations.c: While this is a significant leak, EPA regulations do not require immediate shutdown but rather repair within 30 days.
distractorExplanations.d: The 33% annual leak rate exceeds the substantial leak threshold, requiring faster action than 12 months.

options.a: Keep cylinders in a closed cargo box to shield them from road vibration
options.b: Store cylinders in a shaded, well-ventilated area away from heat sources
options.c: Fill recovery cylinders to 90% so that less vapor space is left to expand
options.d: Lay cylinders on their sides, since horizontal storage lowers pressure

distractorExplanations.a: A closed metal cargo box heats up in the sun and traps vapor; cylinders need shade and ventilation.
distractorExplanations.c: Recovery cylinders must not exceed 80% liquid fill; less vapor space increases the risk of hydrostatic rupture in heat.
distractorExplanations.d: Cylinder pressure depends on temperature, not orientation; cylinders should be secured upright.

options.a: HFCs have zero global warming potential, unlike the CFCs they replaced
options.b: HFCs contain no chlorine atoms and have zero ozone depletion potential
options.c: HFCs are naturally occurring compounds that biodegrade rapidly in air
options.d: HFCs run at lower system pressures, which reduces refrigerant leak rates

distractorExplanations.a: HFCs have substantial GWP (R-134a is about 1,430), which is why the AIM Act now phases them down.
distractorExplanations.c: HFCs are synthetic and many persist in the atmosphere for years; natural refrigerants are ammonia, CO2 and hydrocarbons.
distractorExplanations.d: Many HFCs such as R-410A run at higher pressures than the CFCs they replaced; ozone benefit comes from no chlorine.

epa-608-readiness-check-core-045.explanation: HFCs contain no chlorine atoms, which gives them zero ozone depletion potential (ODP). Chlorine atoms in CFCs are what cause ozone layer destruction when these compounds reach the stratosphere. This absence of chlorine made HFCs suitable transitional replacements under the Montreal Protocol's phase-out of ozone-depleting substances. HFCs have zero ODP precisely because they contain no chlorine.

options.a: The cylinder holds new (virgin) refrigerant and may be refilled only by the manufacturer
options.b: The cylinder is a refillable recovery cylinder for used (recovered) refrigerant
options.c: The cylinder is a disposable cylinder that must be emptied and discarded after one use
options.d: The cylinder holds reclaimed refrigerant certified to AHRI 700 for resale

distractorExplanations.d: Reclaimed refrigerant for resale ships in the refrigerant's own color-coded cylinder, not a gray body with a yellow shoulder.
distractorExplanations.a: New refrigerant is shipped in cylinders color-coded or labeled for the specific refrigerant, not in gray-and-yellow recovery cylinders.
distractorExplanations.c: Disposable (non-refillable) cylinders are for virgin refrigerant and must never be used to recover or refill refrigerant.

epa-608-readiness-check-core-046.explanation: Under the AHRI Guideline K color convention, a gray body with a yellow top/shoulder identifies a refillable recovery cylinder for used refrigerant. Recovery cylinders must never be filled above 80% of capacity by weight, and different refrigerants should not be mixed in the same cylinder, because mixed refrigerant is very difficult to reclaim. Gray-and-yellow cylinders are intended only for holding used, recovered refrigerant.

options.a: Continue normal operation since the leak rate is below the threshold
options.b: Repair the leak within 30 days or develop a retrofit or retirement plan
options.c: Repair the leak within 12 months during the next scheduled maintenance shutdown
options.d: Report the leak to EPA within 30 days and keep operating unrepaired

distractorExplanations.c: Twelve months is not the repair deadline; once the trigger rate is exceeded, repair (or a retrofit/retirement plan) is due within 30 days.
distractorExplanations.d: Reporting alone does not satisfy the rule; exceeding the trigger rate requires repair or a retrofit/retirement plan.
distractorExplanations.a: This is incorrect because 35% exceeds the 15% annual leak rate threshold that triggers mandatory action under EPA regulations.

options.a: Factory-charged, hermetically sealed appliances holding 15 pounds or less of refrigerant
options.b: Manufactured, charged, and hermetically sealed appliances containing 5 pounds or less of refrigerant
options.c: Residential appliances with hermetically sealed compressors and under 50 pounds of refrigerant
options.d: Field-charged split appliances containing 5 pounds or less of refrigerant

distractorExplanations.a: The small-appliance cap is 5 pounds; 15 pounds is the AIM Act leak-repair threshold for HFC appliances.
distractorExplanations.c: 50 pounds is the Section 608 leak-repair threshold, not the small-appliance limit of 5 pounds or less.
distractorExplanations.d: Small appliances must be manufactured, charged and hermetically sealed at the factory; field-charged splits are not included.

options.a: Refrigerant must be recovered to required levels before opening the sealed system
options.b: Refrigerant must be recovered only if it is a CFC or HCFC, and HFCs may be vented
options.c: Venting is permitted as de minimis if the charge is under 5 ounces
options.d: A Type II certification must be held before opening any sealed system

distractorExplanations.b: Since the 2016 rule update, substitutes such as HFCs must also be recovered; HFC venting is prohibited too.
distractorExplanations.c: De minimis covers only unavoidable releases during good-faith recovery, not deliberate venting of a small charge.
distractorExplanations.d: Small appliances are covered by Type I (or Universal) certification; Type II is for high-pressure appliances.

options.a: Small appliances hold more dissolved moisture that must be pulled out
options.b: Small appliances have smaller internal volumes requiring more complete evacuation
options.c: Small appliances run higher-pressure refrigerants that resist vapor transfer to the cylinder
options.d: Small appliances lack service valves, so recovery must remove more oil

distractorExplanations.a: Moisture removal is a dehydration task done before recharge, not the reason for the recovery-level requirement.
distractorExplanations.c: Small appliances use the same common refrigerants as larger systems; refrigerant pressure is not what sets the recovery level.
distractorExplanations.d: Missing service valves are handled with piercing valves; recovery levels target refrigerant, not oil.

options.a: To meet AHRI 700 purity standards for reselling the recovered refrigerant
options.b: To meet EPA recovery efficiency requirements for that appliance type
options.c: To satisfy the UL safety listing required before leak testing begins
options.d: To qualify the technician for Type I certification on that job

distractorExplanations.a: AHRI 700 purity is the reclaimer's job before resale; recovery equipment listing is about recovery efficiency.
distractorExplanations.c: UL listing covers electrical safety; EPA certification of recovery equipment sets recovery efficiency, and leak testing is separate.
distractorExplanations.d: Technician certification comes from passing the Type I test, not from the equipment used on a given job.

options.a: Continue passive recovery for another 30 minutes to reach the required vacuum level
options.b: Switch to active recovery methods to achieve the required 10 inches of mercury vacuum absolute
options.c: Document that recovery is complete since passive methods have achieved maximum extraction
options.d: Add nitrogen to pressurize the system and restart the passive recovery process

distractorExplanations.a: Continuing passive recovery will not achieve a deeper vacuum since the system has already stabilized at 2 inches, which is insufficient for non-functioning compressor requirements.
distractorExplanations.c: While passive methods may have reached their maximum extraction capability, the technician must still meet EPA's 10 inches of mercury vacuum absolute requirement for non-functioning compressors.
distractorExplanations.d: Adding nitrogen would contaminate the refrigerant and is not an approved method for improving recovery efficiency in small appliances.

options.a: Small appliance; recover to 4 inches Hg vacuum using active recovery
options.b: Small appliance; recover to 10 inches Hg vacuum using active recovery
options.c: Not a small appliance; follow Type II procedures
options.d: Small appliance; passive recovery acceptable to any achievable level

distractorExplanations.a: While it is a small appliance, 4 inches Hg vacuum only applies when the compressor is operational.
distractorExplanations.c: 7 ounces is well under the 5-pound limit, so it remains classified as a small appliance under Type I regulations.
distractorExplanations.d: Passive recovery alone is insufficient when active recovery equipment is available and required vacuum levels must still be met.

options.a: No recovery required; refrigerant may be added directly to the operating system
options.b: Partial recovery required to make room for the additional charge
options.c: Complete recovery and a weighed-in recharge are required for any charge adjustment
options.d: Recovery only required if total system charge exceeds 5 pounds after addition

distractorExplanations.c: Adding refrigerant to an operating, leak-free system does not open the circuit, so no recovery is required.
distractorExplanations.b: Partial recovery is not required when adding small amounts (under 2 ounces) during routine maintenance.
distractorExplanations.d: The 2-ounce addition limit applies regardless of the total system charge, as long as the appliance remains classified as a small appliance.

options.a: Convert the vacuum reading to absolute pressure and verify it meets the 4 inches Hg absolute requirement
options.b: Continue recovery until the gauge reads 29.9 inches of mercury vacuum, the level required for R-12
options.c: No additional steps needed - 25 inches vacuum exceeds EPA requirements
options.d: Record the 25-inch reading and convert it to percent recovered, which must reach 95% for R-12

distractorExplanations.b: 29.9 inches Hg vacuum is near a perfect vacuum and is not the small-appliance recovery level for any refrigerant.
distractorExplanations.d: Small-appliance percentage options are 90% (compressor running) or 80% (not running), not 95%.
distractorExplanations.c: This incorrectly assumes 25 inches vacuum is sufficient without converting to absolute pressure measurement.

options.a: System-dependent recovery using the failed compressor
options.b: Self-contained recovery using external recovery equipment
options.c: Recovery to 0 psig only, since R-404A cannot be pulled into a vacuum
options.d: Push-pull liquid recovery, since the charge is above 5 ounces

distractorExplanations.c: R-404A can be recovered into a vacuum; small appliances require 80%/90% recovery or 4 inches Hg vacuum, not 0 psig.
distractorExplanations.d: Push-pull liquid recovery suits large charges with liquid access; an 8-ounce sealed appliance has no liquid to push.
distractorExplanations.a: System-dependent recovery requires a functioning compressor, which is not available in this scenario.

options.a: Vent the 3.5-ounce charge as a de minimis release before brazing
options.b: Recover the refrigerant to required levels before opening the system
options.c: Replace the filter-drier first, then recover what remains in the system
options.d: Pressurize the system with nitrogen over the charge to pinpoint the leak

distractorExplanations.a: Deliberately venting a small charge is not a de minimis release; the refrigerant must be recovered first.
distractorExplanations.c: Cutting out the filter-drier opens the circuit and releases refrigerant; recovery must come before any opening.
distractorExplanations.d: Adding nitrogen on top of refrigerant creates a mixture that is later vented; recover the charge before pressure testing.

options.a: Recover 70% of the charge, the minimum when the compressor will not run
options.b: Recover refrigerant to 4 inches of mercury absolute pressure or lower
options.c: Cut the refrigerant lines and let the 4-ounce charge dissipate outdoors
options.d: Notify EPA within 30 days, then recover the refrigerant at the scrap yard

distractorExplanations.a: With a non-operating compressor the small-appliance requirement is 80% recovery, not 70%.
distractorExplanations.c: Small charges are not exempt from the venting prohibition; refrigerant must be recovered before disposal.
distractorExplanations.d: EPA does not require disposal notification; the refrigerant must be recovered (or recovery verified) before disposal.

options.a: Immediately recover all refrigerant before attempting any repairs
options.b: Repair the leak promptly to minimize refrigerant emissions to the atmosphere
options.c: Replace the entire evaporator coil since brazing repairs are prohibited
options.d: Document the leak location and schedule repair within 30 days

distractorExplanations.a: Complete refrigerant recovery is not always necessary before leak repairs, especially for minor leaks that can be repaired while maintaining system pressure.
distractorExplanations.c: Brazing repairs are acceptable and commonly used for refrigeration system leak repairs when performed by qualified technicians.
distractorExplanations.d: While documentation may be good practice, EPA regulations emphasize prompt repair rather than extended scheduling delays.

options.a: Drain the compressor oil and ship it with the refrigerant for reclaim
options.b: Puncture or remove the compressor to prevent refrigerant accumulation
options.c: Flush the system with nitrogen to remove all refrigerant traces
options.d: Install locking caps on the service ports to deter refrigerant theft

distractorExplanations.a: Reclaimers process refrigerant, not compressor oil; draining oil is not the disposal step being asked about.
distractorExplanations.d: Locking caps are a building-code anti-tamper measure for outdoor units, not a disposal step for a small appliance.
distractorExplanations.c: System flushing is not required for disposal preparation under EPA regulations for small appliances.

options.a: System-dependent recovery using the operating compressor
options.b: Self-contained recovery, required whenever leaks are present
options.c: Push-pull liquid recovery using a second recovery cylinder
options.d: No recovery, since a leaking system counts as already evacuated

distractorExplanations.b: Leaks do not mandate self-contained equipment; with a working compressor, system-dependent recovery is allowed.
distractorExplanations.c: Push-pull needs a large liquid charge and liquid access; an 8-ounce small appliance has neither.
distractorExplanations.d: A low-charge leaking system still holds refrigerant that must be recovered before it is opened or disposed of.

options.a: Continue recovery until reaching 4 inches of mercury vacuum absolute
options.b: Release the unit for disposal, since 6 inches meets the small-appliance level
options.c: Wait 5 minutes, and if the reading holds, release the unit for disposal
options.d: Switch to system-dependent recovery and pull to 10 inches of mercury

distractorExplanations.b: The small-appliance level is 4 inches Hg vacuum; the 6-inch reading does not meet it yet.
distractorExplanations.c: A stable reading does not matter if the required level has not been reached; recovery must continue first.
distractorExplanations.d: 10 inches Hg vacuum is a high-pressure appliance level, and switching methods does not change the small-appliance target.

options.a: Document the leak but continue service since it's minor
options.b: Repair the leak before completing any other service work
options.c: Recover the charge and report the leak to EPA within 30 days
options.d: Add refrigerant to compensate for the leak and finish the coil cleaning

distractorExplanations.c: EPA has no 30-day leak report for small appliances; the 30-day clock applies to larger appliances over the trigger rate.
distractorExplanations.d: Topping off a known leak lets refrigerant keep escaping; the leak should be fixed before the charge is restored.
distractorExplanations.a: Simply documenting a leak without repair violates EPA requirements - all detected leaks must be repaired during service.

options.a: System-dependent recovery only, using the operating compressor
options.b: Self-contained recovery equipment, since the charge exceeds 4 ounces
options.c: Either system-dependent or self-contained recovery equipment
options.d: Push-pull liquid recovery with a dedicated recovery cylinder

distractorExplanations.a: System-dependent recovery is allowed but not exclusive; self-contained equipment is equally acceptable here.
distractorExplanations.b: There is no 4-ounce cutoff; with a running compressor either system-dependent or self-contained equipment may be used.
distractorExplanations.d: Push-pull requires a large liquid charge with liquid access; a 5-ounce wine cooler has no usable liquid line.

options.a: System-dependent recovery equipment certified to recover 70% of refrigerant
options.b: Self-contained recovery equipment certified to recover 95% of refrigerant
options.c: Any recovery equipment capable of achieving 15 inches mercury vacuum
options.d: Passive recovery methods are sufficient due to operating compressor

distractorExplanations.a: 70% is not an EPA small-appliance recovery level; the options are 80% or 90% depending on compressor status.
distractorExplanations.c: The vacuum level requirement is secondary to using proper self-contained equipment for appliances over 10 ounces.
distractorExplanations.d: Passive recovery is never sufficient for appliances containing more than 10 ounces of refrigerant, regardless of compressor operation.

options.a: Recovery is complete, since 8 inches absolute already beats the 10-inch level
options.b: Wait 5 minutes, then pull vacuum to 15 inches mercury absolute
options.c: Wait 5 minutes, then verify vacuum holds at 10 inches mercury absolute or higher
options.d: Immediately achieve 4 inches mercury absolute vacuum level

distractorExplanations.a: The reading has not been confirmed to hold after a 5-minute wait, so recovery cannot be called complete yet.
distractorExplanations.b: The target vacuum level of 15 inches mercury absolute is incorrect - the verification should confirm the vacuum has not risen above 10 inches mercury absolute.
distractorExplanations.d: A vacuum level of 4 inches mercury absolute is the requirement for inoperative compressors, not for systems with operating compressors using system-dependent recovery.

options.a: Recover only the liquid charge, leaving vapor in the circuit for repair
options.b: Recover refrigerant to required vacuum levels using approved equipment
options.c: Vent the vapor after recovering liquid, since vapor holds little refrigerant
options.d: Add a nitrogen holding charge, then open the system without recovery

distractorExplanations.a: Vapor left in the circuit is released when the system is opened; recovery must reach the required vacuum level.
distractorExplanations.c: Vapor still contains regulated refrigerant and venting it is prohibited; it must be recovered to the required level.
distractorExplanations.d: A nitrogen holding charge is added after recovery; it does not replace removing the refrigerant first.

options.a: Recover refrigerant to atmospheric pressure
options.b: Recover refrigerant to 15 inches of mercury vacuum
options.c: Recover refrigerant to 10 inches of mercury vacuum or lower
options.d: Recover refrigerant until the low-side gauge reads 5 psig

distractorExplanations.d: 5 psig is still positive pressure, so refrigerant would escape when the coil is opened.
distractorExplanations.a: Recovering only to atmospheric pressure leaves significant refrigerant in the system that would be released during repairs.
distractorExplanations.b: 15 inches of mercury vacuum does not meet the EPA requirement for Type II appliances, which is 10 inches or lower.

options.a: The recovery cylinder is full and should be replaced with an empty cylinder
options.b: Liquid refrigerant has pooled in the evaporator and the system should be heated
options.c: The recovery machine filter is clogged and needs replacement
options.d: The compressor has failed, so recovery should stop at the current positive pressure

distractorExplanations.d: Stopping at positive pressure leaves refrigerant in the system; slow transfer at positive pressure points to pooled liquid.
distractorExplanations.a: A full recovery cylinder would typically cause high pressure warnings or automatic shutoff, not just slow recovery with remaining system pressure.
distractorExplanations.c: While a clogged filter could slow recovery, it wouldn't typically leave positive pressure in the system if recovery had been proceeding normally.

options.a: Recovery can only be performed when outdoor temperature exceeds 70°F
options.b: The process relies on pressure differential and may not achieve complete removal
options.c: Passive recovery is prohibited on systems containing more than 15 pounds of refrigerant
options.d: The recovery cylinder must be heated to at least 100°F throughout the process

distractorExplanations.a: Outdoor temperature requirements are not specified for passive recovery methods, though temperature affects pressure differentials.
distractorExplanations.c: There is no EPA prohibition on passive recovery based on refrigerant charge size, though it may be impractical for larger systems.
distractorExplanations.d: Heating the recovery cylinder is not a requirement for passive recovery and could be dangerous by increasing cylinder pressure.

options.a: Recover 80% of the refrigerant charge by weight
options.b: Recover 90% of the refrigerant charge by weight
options.c: Recover 95% of the refrigerant charge by weight
options.d: Evacuate to 10 inches of mercury vacuum

distractorExplanations.a: 80% is a small-appliance level for a non-operating compressor, not the Type II disposal requirement.
distractorExplanations.b: 90% is a small-appliance level for an operating compressor; Type II disposal uses a vacuum level.
distractorExplanations.c: Type II recovery is defined by an inches-of-mercury vacuum level, not a 95% weight percentage.

options.a: Recover through the system's own compressor to keep acid out of the machine
options.b: The recovered refrigerant must be reclaimed due to acid contamination
options.c: Recover only the vapor, since acid stays behind in the liquid refrigerant
options.d: Double the normal evacuation time to ensure complete recovery

distractorExplanations.a: A burned-out hermetic compressor cannot run, so system-dependent recovery through it is not possible.
distractorExplanations.c: Acid is carried in both liquid and oil; all refrigerant must be recovered and the contaminated charge sent for reclaim.
distractorExplanations.d: Extended evacuation time alone does not address the contamination issue that requires reclamation.

options.a: No recovery required since the repair can be completed in under 30 minutes
options.b: Recover refrigerant to 0 psig vacuum level before opening the system
options.c: Recover refrigerant to 10 inches of mercury vacuum before opening the system
options.d: Only recover refrigerant from the condenser section being replaced

distractorExplanations.a: Recovery is always required before opening refrigerant circuits for major repairs, regardless of repair time.
distractorExplanations.b: 0 psig is not sufficient; a specific vacuum level must be achieved to ensure proper recovery.
distractorExplanations.d: The entire system must be recovered to the required vacuum level, not just the component being replaced.

options.a: The system has leaked its charge, so it can be opened after a 0 psig gauge check
options.b: The gauges are reading falsely low, so the system should be pressurized with nitrogen first
options.c: Refrigerant may have condensed in the evaporator and recovery should still be attempted
options.d: The charge has migrated to the compressor crankcase, so only the oil needs recovery

distractorExplanations.a: A 0 psig reading does not prove the system is empty; refrigerant can remain and recovery must still be attempted.
distractorExplanations.b: Adding nitrogen to a system that may still hold refrigerant creates a mixture that is later vented.
distractorExplanations.d: Refrigerant dissolved in oil or condensed in the evaporator still has to be recovered, not just the oil.

options.a: Switch to active recovery equipment to achieve required vacuum levels
options.b: Heat the recovery cylinder to raise its pressure and speed the transfer
options.c: Continue passive recovery until system and cylinder pressures equalize
options.d: Add nitrogen to the system to push remaining refrigerant out

distractorExplanations.c: Equalized pressure still leaves the system at about 40 psig of refrigerant; passive transfer cannot reach the required vacuum.
distractorExplanations.b: Heating the receiving cylinder raises its pressure and slows transfer; the recovery cylinder should be kept cool.
distractorExplanations.d: Adding nitrogen during recovery contaminates the refrigerant and violates proper recovery procedures.

options.a: Recover refrigerant from the entire system to 15 inches Hg vacuum
options.b: Pump the charge into the condenser and open the liquid line while it still reads 5 psig
options.c: Isolate and recover refrigerant from the liquid line to atmospheric pressure
options.d: No recovery required if the repair can be completed in under 15 minutes

distractorExplanations.b: Opening at 5 psig still releases refrigerant; the isolated section must be recovered to at least atmospheric pressure.
distractorExplanations.a: Full system recovery to 15 inches Hg vacuum is not required for minor component replacement when the section can be properly isolated.
distractorExplanations.d: Time limits do not exempt the requirement for proper refrigerant recovery before opening any pressurized system components.

options.a: Recovery is complete since proper vacuum level has been achieved
options.b: The sight glass shows trapped oil, not refrigerant, so recovery can stop
options.c: Recovery should continue until no liquid is visible in the sight glass
options.d: Switch to passive recovery methods to complete the process

distractorExplanations.b: Visible liquid in the sight glass means refrigerant is still present; recovery should continue until it clears.
distractorExplanations.a: Vacuum level alone does not indicate complete recovery; liquid refrigerant remaining in the system means more recovery is needed.
distractorExplanations.d: Active recovery should be continued rather than switching methods, as it is more effective for removing remaining liquid refrigerant.

options.a: No recovery, since filter-drier and accumulator swaps count as routine maintenance
options.b: Recover refrigerant from the components being replaced
options.c: Recover refrigerant to 0 psig throughout the entire system
options.d: Recover refrigerant to 15 inches of mercury vacuum throughout the entire system

distractorExplanations.a: Calling the job routine does not exempt it; opening the circuit requires recovery to the required vacuum level.
distractorExplanations.b: Partial recovery is not permitted; the entire interconnected refrigerant system must be properly evacuated before opening any connections.
distractorExplanations.c: Zero psig is insufficient for Type II appliances; the EPA requires achieving 15 inches of mercury vacuum for active recovery methods.

options.a: Continue recovery until 10 inches of mercury vacuum is achieved
options.b: Stop recovery as the system is sufficiently evacuated
options.c: Switch to passive recovery to draw out the remaining vapor
options.d: Add heat to the system to vaporize remaining refrigerant

distractorExplanations.c: Passive recovery relies on pressure differential and cannot pull a system from 12 psig into the required vacuum.
distractorExplanations.b: The system at 12 psig has not reached the required 10 inches of mercury vacuum for Type II appliances, so recovery must continue.
distractorExplanations.d: While heat can help vaporize refrigerant, the primary requirement is to continue active recovery until the proper vacuum level is achieved.

options.a: It lowers condenser pressure below the chiller's design setpoint
options.b: It can release regulated refrigerant mixed with the non-condensables
options.c: It voids the pressure rating of the rupture disc on the chiller's evaporator shell
options.d: It is banned because air itself is a regulated ozone-depleting gas

distractorExplanations.a: Removing air actually helps condenser pressure; the prohibition is about refrigerant released with the air.
distractorExplanations.c: Purging does not affect the rupture disc; the issue is regulated refrigerant escaping with the non-condensables.
distractorExplanations.d: Air is not regulated; venting is restricted because refrigerant is mixed in with the non-condensables.

options.a: Passive recovery using only system pressure differentials
options.b: Heat application to the evaporator combined with mechanical recovery
options.c: Nitrogen pressurization to push vapor into a standard recovery cylinder
options.d: Gravity drainage through the lowest system connection point

distractorExplanations.c: Pressurizing with nitrogen mixes it with the vapor and risks the 15 psig rupture disc; heat plus mechanical recovery is used.
distractorExplanations.a: Passive recovery alone cannot achieve the low vacuum levels required for proper recovery from low-pressure systems due to insufficient pressure differential.
distractorExplanations.d: Gravity drainage would only remove liquid refrigerant and cannot achieve the vapor recovery levels required by EPA regulations.

options.a: Self-contained units with air-cooled condensers rated for R-410A
options.b: System-dependent recovery equipment with vacuum pump assistance
options.c: Passive recovery bags without active pumping or a condenser
options.d: Standard high-pressure recovery machines rated for 400 psig cylinders

distractorExplanations.a: High-pressure, air-cooled R-410A units are not suited to pulling low-pressure refrigerant from a deep-vacuum chiller.
distractorExplanations.c: Passive bags are a small-appliance technique and cannot reach the deep vacuum levels set for low-pressure chillers.
distractorExplanations.d: High-pressure machines are not designed for the sub-atmospheric conditions and large liquid volumes of low-pressure chillers.

options.a: To increase system efficiency by removing excess refrigerant
options.b: To remove non-condensable gases that leak into the system
options.c: To maintain proper oil circulation throughout the system
options.d: To relieve high-side pressure when the condenser water fails

distractorExplanations.d: High-side overpressure is handled by the rupture disc and safety controls, not by the purge unit.
distractorExplanations.a: Air purge units remove air and non-condensables, not excess refrigerant, and this actually improves rather than reduces efficiency.
distractorExplanations.c: Oil circulation is managed by oil pumps and system design, not by air purge units.

epa-608-readiness-check-type-3-009.explanation: Low-pressure chillers operate below atmospheric pressure, which allows air and other non-condensable gases to leak into the system through small openings. Air purge units automatically remove these gases to maintain system efficiency and prevent damage. Air leaks in because the chiller operates below atmospheric pressure.

options.a: Pressurize the system with nitrogen to 150 psig for a leak test
options.b: Leave the machine in a deep vacuum while it stays open for the repair work
options.c: Break the vacuum with nitrogen to prevent atmospheric contamination
options.d: Immediately seal all openings with refrigerant-rated tape

distractorExplanations.a: Low-pressure chillers have a rupture disc near 15 psig; test pressure is limited to about 10 psig, not 150.
distractorExplanations.b: An opened machine cannot hold a vacuum; leaving it under vacuum draws air and moisture into the shell.
distractorExplanations.d: While sealing openings is good practice, breaking the vacuum with nitrogen is the specific procedure for low-pressure systems.

options.a: Large refrigerant charges held in the evaporator shell
options.b: Evaporator operating below atmospheric pressure
options.c: Condenser operating above atmospheric pressure
options.d: Water-cooled condensers with large tube surface areas

distractorExplanations.a: Charge size affects how much can leak out, but air gets in because the evaporator runs below atmospheric pressure.
distractorExplanations.c: A condenser above atmospheric pressure leaks refrigerant out, not air in; the evaporator below atmosphere draws air in.
distractorExplanations.d: Condenser surface area affects heat rejection, not non-condensable entry, which comes from sub-atmospheric operation.

options.a: Risk of refrigerant vapor explosion due to flammability
options.b: Air and moisture entering the system creating contamination
options.c: Sudden pressure equalization causing component damage
options.d: Release of high-pressure refrigerant causing injury

distractorExplanations.a: Most refrigerants used in low-pressure appliances (like R-123) are not flammable, and explosion risk is not the primary concern when opening to atmosphere.
distractorExplanations.c: Since low-pressure appliances operate below atmospheric pressure, opening to atmosphere actually increases internal pressure gradually rather than causing sudden decompression.
distractorExplanations.d: Low-pressure appliances operate below atmospheric pressure, so there is no high-pressure refrigerant release when opened to atmosphere.

options.a: To prevent moisture contamination of the recovered refrigerant
options.b: To prevent air from entering the recovery system
options.c: To maintain proper oil separation during the recovery process
options.d: To keep recovered R-123 below its 50 ppm occupational exposure limit

distractorExplanations.d: Exposure limits are managed by ventilation and monitors; sealed recovery equipment is about keeping air out.
distractorExplanations.a: While moisture prevention is important, the primary concern with low-pressure systems is air infiltration due to the vacuum conditions, not moisture specifically.
distractorExplanations.c: Oil separation is a consideration in recovery but not the primary reason for requiring hermetically sealed equipment in low-pressure applications.

epa-608-readiness-check-type-3-026.explanation: Low-pressure appliances operate below atmospheric pressure, creating a vacuum that would draw air into any non-sealed recovery equipment. Air contamination would make the recovered refrigerant unusable and violate EPA requirements for proper refrigerant handling. Air entering the recovery system contaminates the refrigerant.

options.a: A complete system pressure test at maximum working pressure
options.b: Evacuation to remove air and moisture that entered during service
options.c: Replacement of every gasket and seal disturbed during the repair
options.d: Installation of a refrigerant monitor and alarm in the mechanical equipment room

distractorExplanations.c: Gaskets are replaced only when damaged; the step required before recharge is evacuation of air and moisture.
distractorExplanations.d: Machine-room monitors are an ASHRAE 15 safety requirement, not the pre-charge step after opening the system.
distractorExplanations.a: While pressure testing may be performed, it's not the critical step required after atmospheric exposure - evacuation to remove air and moisture is essential.

options.a: Low-pressure appliances are exempt from charge calculation requirements
options.b: The full charge must include refrigerant in the evaporator but exclude condenser inventory
options.c: The full charge includes all refrigerant in the appliance and receiver tank
options.d: Only the refrigerant in the compressor and associated piping counts toward the full charge

distractorExplanations.a: Low-pressure appliances are not exempt from charge calculations - they must comply with the same EPA recordkeeping and leak rate requirements as other systems.
distractorExplanations.b: The full charge calculation includes refrigerant in both the evaporator and condenser, not just the evaporator portion of the system.
distractorExplanations.d: The full charge includes much more than just compressor and piping - it encompasses the entire system refrigerant inventory during operation.

epa-608-readiness-check-type-3-028.explanation: For low-pressure appliances, the full charge calculation includes all refrigerant in the complete system including the receiver tank when the system is operating. This comprehensive approach accounts for the large refrigerant inventory typical in these systems. It is measured with the appliance operating.

options.a: There is no time limit specified
options.b: 4 hours continuous operation
options.c: 8 hours continuous operation
options.d: 24 hours of continuous machine operation

distractorExplanations.d: EPA sets recovery levels, not a run-time limit; 24 hours is not a regulated shutdown point.
distractorExplanations.b: A 4-hour limit is not specified in EPA regulations for low-pressure appliance recovery.
distractorExplanations.c: An 8-hour limit is not established by EPA regulations for recovery operations.

options.a: Slightly above atmospheric on the low side and well above it on the high side
options.b: Below atmospheric pressure on the low side, above atmospheric on the high side
options.c: Below atmospheric pressure on both high and low sides
options.d: At atmospheric pressure on the low side, above atmospheric on the high side

distractorExplanations.a: Low-pressure chillers run their evaporator below atmospheric pressure, which is why air leaks in.
distractorExplanations.c: While the low side operates below atmospheric pressure, the high side must be above atmospheric to reject heat effectively.
distractorExplanations.d: The low side operates below atmospheric pressure, not at atmospheric pressure, which is what creates the vacuum condition.

options.a: High-pressure refrigerant will escape rapidly into the room
options.b: Air and moisture will enter the refrigerant system
options.c: The compressor will overheat immediately
options.d: Electrical components will short circuit

distractorExplanations.a: The evaporator runs below atmospheric pressure, so a leak draws air in rather than blowing refrigerant out.
distractorExplanations.c: While contamination can eventually cause compressor problems, immediate overheating is not the primary concern with evaporator leaks.
distractorExplanations.d: Evaporator coil leaks don't directly cause electrical short circuits, though moisture contamination could eventually affect electrical components.

options.a: Replace the float metering valve and its seals
options.b: Evacuate the system to remove air and moisture
options.c: Add refrigerant vapor first to sweep out the air
options.d: Test the compressor motor windings

distractorExplanations.a: The metering device is replaced only if faulty; the required step is evacuation to remove air and moisture.
distractorExplanations.c: Sweeping with refrigerant vents it along with the air; the system must be evacuated instead.
distractorExplanations.d: Testing compressor windings is good practice but evacuation to remove air and moisture is the mandatory step before recharging.

options.a: Monitor the system for pressure rise during the off cycle
options.b: Sniff for refrigerant with an electronic detector at the evaporator
options.c: Measure the vacuum level with a micron gauge
options.d: Observe frost formation on the evaporator coils

distractorExplanations.b: A sub-atmospheric evaporator leaks air inward, so a detector at the shell finds little; watch for pressure rise when off.
distractorExplanations.c: While micron gauges measure vacuum levels, they don't specifically indicate leaks during normal operation - the pressure rise test is the standard leak detection method.
distractorExplanations.d: Frost formation indicates normal operation or other issues like low refrigerant charge, not necessarily leaks in low-pressure systems.

options.a: Wear chemical-resistant gloves due to refrigerant toxicity
options.b: Ensure adequate ventilation to prevent refrigerant accumulation
options.c: Use only spark-proof tools to prevent ignition
options.d: Install temporary pressure relief devices

distractorExplanations.a: While good practice, the primary safety concern with low-pressure refrigerants is asphyxiation risk rather than skin contact toxicity.
distractorExplanations.c: Low-pressure refrigerants are typically non-flammable, so spark-proof tools are not the primary safety requirement.
distractorExplanations.d: Low-pressure systems operate below atmospheric pressure, so pressure relief is not the main concern during opening for repairs.

options.a: 500 microns of mercury absolute
options.b: 1000 microns of mercury absolute
options.c: 10 millimeters of mercury absolute
options.d: 15 inches of mercury vacuum

distractorExplanations.a: 500 microns is the common high-pressure dehydration target, not the level given for low-pressure appliances.
distractorExplanations.b: 1000 microns is a field rule of thumb for dehydration checks, not the level given for low-pressure appliances.
distractorExplanations.d: 15 inches of mercury vacuum is not deep enough and uses incorrect units for low-pressure appliance specifications.

options.a: They contain larger refrigerant charges that increase leak potential
options.b: They operate below atmospheric pressure, allowing air and moisture infiltration
options.c: They use R-123, which has a higher ozone depletion potential than R-11
options.d: They operate above atmospheric pressure, which forces refrigerant out through leaks

distractorExplanations.c: R-11 has an ODP of 1.0 while R-123 is about 0.02; R-123 replaced R-11 to cut ozone damage.
distractorExplanations.d: That describes high-pressure systems; low-pressure appliances run below atmosphere and pull air and moisture in.
distractorExplanations.a: While low-pressure appliances often have large charges, the pressure differential is the primary environmental concern, not just charge size.

options.a: They improve heat transfer once mixed evenly with the refrigerant vapor
options.b: They cause excessive refrigerant consumption during normal operation
options.c: They impair system performance and must be removed through proper evacuation
options.d: They are removed by the purge unit during operation, so evacuation can be skipped

distractorExplanations.a: Non-condensables blanket condenser tubes and reduce heat transfer, raising head pressure.
distractorExplanations.d: The purge unit handles small in-leaks during operation; after opening, the system must still be evacuated.
distractorExplanations.b: While non-condensables affect performance, they don't directly cause refrigerant consumption issues during normal operation.

options.a: Low-pressure centrifugal chillers
options.b: Domestic chest freezers
options.c: Motor vehicle air conditioners
options.d: Window room air conditioners

distractorExplanations.b: Chest freezers are small appliances under Type I.
distractorExplanations.c: Motor vehicle A/C has separate EPA requirements; Type III targets low-pressure stationary equipment.
distractorExplanations.d: Window units are Type I small appliances.

options.a: To an EPA-certified reclaimer, distributor, or recycler
options.b: Directly to a municipal landfill if the charge is under 1 pound
options.c: To any scrap yard, which will reclaim it to AHRI 700 standards
options.d: Back to the appliance manufacturer, who holds the reclaim license

distractorExplanations.c: Scrap yards are final processors for appliances, not certified reclaimers that purify refrigerant to AHRI 700.
distractorExplanations.d: Manufacturers do not hold reclaim certification; refrigerant goes to an EPA-certified reclaimer or approved handler.
distractorExplanations.b: Landfill disposal of refrigerant cylinders or vented refrigerant is not permitted.

epa-608-readiness-check-type-1-048.explanation: Recovered refrigerant must be handled by certified reclaimers or approved recipients; intentional venting is prohibited. The destination must be approved to accept the recovered refrigerant.

options.a: To prevent accidental use of the wrong refrigerant on an R-410A system
options.b: Because R-410A must be charged as vapor, and the valve meters vapor flow
options.c: To increase recovery speed on high-pressure systems
options.d: Because left-hand threads hold R-410A's higher pressure without leaking

distractorExplanations.b: R-410A is a zeotropic blend charged as liquid; thread direction has nothing to do with vapor metering.
distractorExplanations.d: Thread direction does not change pressure rating; cylinder pressure capacity comes from DOT cylinder specification.
distractorExplanations.c: Thread orientation is a safety and compatibility measure, not a recovery-speed feature.

options.a: After confirming the test pressure is released to atmosphere with no mixed refrigerant present
options.b: Only after the nitrogen is recovered into a gray-and-yellow recovery cylinder
options.c: After venting any refrigerant left in the system together with the nitrogen test charge
options.d: When the test pressure is under 150 psig, even if refrigerant was mixed in

distractorExplanations.b: Pure nitrogen is not a regulated refrigerant and does not need recovery; recovery cylinders are for used refrigerant.
distractorExplanations.c: Refrigerant mixed into the test gas is not de minimis; venting it with the nitrogen violates the venting prohibition.
distractorExplanations.d: Test pressure does not make a refrigerant/nitrogen mixture ventable; any refrigerant present must be recovered.

epa-608-readiness-check-type-2-017.explanation: Dry nitrogen used for leak testing may be vented after the test if no regulated refrigerant is mixed with it and safe venting practices are followed. Release it in a ventilated area.

options.a: To prevent air and moisture from entering the system through leaks
options.b: To keep the rupture disc seated and sealed during extended shutdown periods
options.c: To allow direct venting of non-condensables without recovery
options.d: To stop refrigerant migrating to the condenser while idle

distractorExplanations.b: The rupture disc is a relief device set near 15 psig; slight positive pressure is about keeping air out, not seating it.
distractorExplanations.d: Migration is a temperature effect not prevented by pressurizing; the goal is to stop air and moisture leaking in.
distractorExplanations.c: Non-condensables must still be handled without venting regulated refrigerant.

epa-608-readiness-check-type-3-002.explanation: Low-pressure systems operate below atmospheric pressure on the evaporator side; positive pressure during shutdown reduces air and moisture ingress that causes acids and non-condensables. Low-pressure chillers leak inward on the low side.

options.a: Warm the refrigerant and start recovery from the proper low-side access
options.b: Run the purge unit to vent the refrigerant vapor before opening the shell
options.c: Pressurize the shell with nitrogen to 50 psig to push out the liquid
options.d: Drain the oil from the sump first, then recover the vapor from the condenser

distractorExplanations.b: The purge unit removes non-condensables, not the charge; using it to vent refrigerant is prohibited.
distractorExplanations.c: 50 psig exceeds the roughly 15 psig rupture disc on a low-pressure chiller and mixes nitrogen into the refrigerant.
distractorExplanations.d: Oil holds dissolved refrigerant and is removed after recovery; recovery starts with the refrigerant charge.

epa-608-readiness-check-type-3-016.explanation: Low-pressure chiller recovery often requires controlled heating to boil refrigerant off the evaporator bundle and route vapor for recovery because the machine operates below atmospheric pressure on the low side. Warming drives vapor into the condenser for recovery.

options.a: Pressurize with dry nitrogen and soap-bubble test before pulling a deep vacuum
options.b: Pressurize with R-123 vapor to 50 psig and sniff the gasket with a detector
options.c: Pressurize with compressed shop air and soap-bubble test the joints before charging
options.d: Leak test at 25 psig of nitrogen to stress the new gasket before charging

distractorExplanations.b: 50 psig exceeds the low-pressure rupture disc, and refrigerant should not be used as a pressurizing test gas.
distractorExplanations.c: Shop air carries moisture and oxygen into the chiller; dry nitrogen is the required pressurizing gas.
distractorExplanations.d: 25 psig exceeds the roughly 15 psig rupture disc; low-pressure chillers are tested at about 10 psig or less.

epa-608-readiness-check-type-3-025.explanation: After major repairs, technicians leak test with an inert trace gas such as nitrogen, then evacuate and charge; intentional refrigerant venting for leak detection is prohibited. Charge only after the vacuum.
